claim: By bioinformatic analysis of a human PCSC-enriched gene signature, the transcription factor HNF1A was identified as a putative central regulator of PCSC function.
source: By bioinformatic analysis of a human PCSC-enriched gene signature, we identified the transcription factor HNF1A as a putative central regulator of PCSC function.
evidence: The claim is supported by the bioinformatic analysis described in the manuscript, including microarray data and oPOSSUM analysis showing HNF1A binding sites in PCSC-enriched genes.

claim: Levels of HNF1A and its target genes were found to be elevated in PCSCs and tumorspheres.
source: Levels of HNF1A and its target genes were found to be elevated in PCSCs and tumorspheres
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR, Western blot, and flow cytometry data showing elevated HNF1A expression in P2 subpopulations and tumorsphere conditions.

claim: Depletion of HNF1A resulted in growth inhibition in PDA cells.
source: depletion of HNF1A resulted in growth inhibition
evidence: The claim is supported by cell counting experiments showing reduced cell numbers following HNF1A knockdown.

claim: Depletion of HNF1A resulted in apoptosis in PDA cells.
source: depletion of HNF1A resulted in growth inhibition, apoptosis
evidence: The claim is supported by annexin V staining and cleaved caspase Western blots showing increased apoptosis following HNF1A knockdown.

claim: Depletion of HNF1A resulted in impaired tumorsphere formation.
source: depletion of HNF1A resulted in growth inhibition, apoptosis, impaired tumorsphere formation
evidence: The claim is supported by tumorsphere assays showing reduced sphere formation following HNF1A knockdown.

claim: Depletion of HNF1A resulted in decreased PCSC marker expression.

claim: Depletion of HNF1A resulted in downregulation of POU5F1/OCT4 expression.

evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR and Western blot data showing reduced POU5F1/OCT4 expression following HNF1A knockdown.

claim: HNF1A overexpression increased PCSC marker expression in pancreatic cancer cells.
source: Conversely, HNF1A overexpression increased PCSC marker expression and tumorsphere formation in pancreatic cancer cells
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased CD24, CD44, and EPCAM expression following doxycycline-induced HNF1A expression.

claim: HNF1A overexpression increased tumorsphere formation in pancreatic cancer cells.
source: Conversely, HNF1A overexpression increased PCSC marker expression and tumorsphere formation in pancreatic cancer cells
evidence: The claim is supported by tumorsphere assays showing increased sphere formation following HNF1A overexpression.

claim: HNF1A overexpression drove pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) cell growth.
source: HNF1A overexpression increased PCSC marker expression and tumorsphere formation in pancreatic cancer cells and drove pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) cell growth.
evidence: The claim is supported by colony formation and soft agar assays showing increased growth following HNF1A overexpression.

claim: Depletion of HNF1A in xenografts impaired tumor growth.
source: Importantly, depletion of HNF1A in xenografts impaired tumor growth

claim: Depletion of HNF1A in xenografts depleted PCSC marker-positive cells in vivo.

evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry analysis of dissociated tumors showing reduced EPCAM+/CD44+/CD24+ cells following HNF1A knockdown.

claim: An HNF1A-dependent gene signature in PDA cells significantly correlated with reduced survivability in patients.
source: Finally, we established an HNF1A-dependent gene signature in PDA cells that significantly correlated with reduced survivability in patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by Cox proportional hazards survival analysis of TCGA data showing that HNF1A upregulated genes are associated with poor patient survival.

claim: HNF1A is a central transcriptional regulator of PCSC properties.

In all cases, knockdown of HNF1A resulted in a significant (p<0.05) increase in apoptotic cells, while not affecting necrotic cell numbers (Figure 2D, data not shown).

source: HNF1A alone resulted in significantly increased colony formation, which was further enhanced by the additional expression of KRASG12D.

claim: HNF1A-expressing HPNE cells formed similar numbers of colonies to control and KRASG12D-expressing cells in clonogenicity assays.

claim: HPDE cells failed to form colonies at clonal densities in the presence of serum.
source: HPDE cells failed to form colonies at clonal densities in the presence of serum.

claim: HNF1A-depleted NY5 and NY15 cells showed significantly reduced tumor growth compared to their control cohorts (p<0.05) in orthotopic xenografts.
source: To determine whether HNF1A was necessary for tumorigenesis, we implanted two HNF1A-high primary lines (NY5 and NY15) expressing control or two HNF1A-targeting shRNAs orthotopically in the pancreas of NOD/SCID mice. HNF1A-depleted cells showed significantly reduced tumor growth compared to their control cohorts (p<0.05), (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by orthotopic xenograft data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Similar results to orthotopic xenografts were observed with HNF1A knockdown in subcutaneous xenografts of NY5 and NY15 cells.

evidence: The claim is supported by subcutaneous xenograft data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The EPCAM+/CD44+/CD24+ cell population was significantly reduced in HNF1A-depleted NY5 tumors (p<0.05).
source: To determine whether inhibition of tumor growth was due to effects on the PCSC compartment, NY5 tumors were dissociated and analyzed by flow cytometry. Consistent with our in vitro findings, the EPCAM+/CD44+/CD24 +cell population was significantly reduced in HNF1A-depleted tumors (p<0.05) (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data from dissociated tumors shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: Western blot analysis of tumor lysates confirmed that shRNAs remained effective at depleting HNF1A during the course of the xenograft experiment.

evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only POU5F1/OCT4 mRNA showed consistent downregulation in multiple PDA cell lines in response to HNF1A knockdown among the central stemness regulators MYC, SOX2, KLF4, NANOG, and POU5F1/OCT4.
source: As a direct relationship between HNF1A and stem cell function has not been reported, we examined mRNA expression of central stemness regulators MYC, SOX2, KLF4, NANOG, and POU5F1/OCT4 in HNF1A-depleted cells. Of these transcription factors, only POU5F1/OCT4 mRNA showed consistent downregulation in multiple PDA cell lines in response to HNF1A knockdown (Figure 6A, data not shown).

claim: POU5F1/OCT4 mRNA was upregulated in response to overexpression of HNF1A in both PDA cells and HPDE cells.
source: Similarly, we found that POU5F1/OCT4 mRNA was upregulated in response to overexpression of HNF1A in both PDA cells and HPDE cells (Figure 6B)
evidence: The claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HNF1A regulates POU5F1/OCT4 expression in pancreatic-lineage cells.

The Pearson correlation coefficient of POU5F1/OCT4 mRNA was found to be significantly correlated (p=0.0094) with HNF1A mRNA levels (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: POU5F1/OCT4 and HNF1A mRNA levels were correlated (Pearson's r = 0.406, p=8.9×10−8) in patient tumor samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) dataset for PDA (PAAD cohort).

evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data.

claim: There was no significant association between POU5F1/OCT4 mRNA and any of the PDA subpopulations.

evidence: The claim is supported by unpublished data mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Factors other than HNF1A modulate the levels of POU5F1/OCT4 mRNA in different PDA subpopulations.
source: indicating that factors other than HNF1A modulate the levels of POU5F1/OCT4 mRNA in different PDA subpopulations (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of the lack of correlation between POU5F1/OCT4 mRNA and subpopulations.

claim: Previously published HNF1A ChIP-seq data performed in HepG2 cells by ENCODE identified a region of enrichment of HNF1A upstream of the POU5F1/PSORS1C3 gene loci proximal to a recently identified retrotransposon long terminal repeat (LTR)-rich region.
source: Previously published HNF1A chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) data performed in HepG2 cells by The Encyclopedia of DNA Elements (ENCODE) project (Consortium and ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) identified a region of enrichment of HNF1A upstream of the POU5F1/PSORS1C3 gene loci proximal to recently identified retrotransposon long terminal repeat (LTR)-rich region that can serve as a promoter for both genes (Malakootian et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Consortium and ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012 and Malakootian et al., 2017.

claim: The LTR promoter region can serve as a promoter for both POU5F1 and PSORS1C3 genes.
source: proximal to recently identified retrotransposon long terminal repeat (LTR)-rich region that can serve as a promoter for both genes (Malakootian et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Malakootian et al., 2017.

claim: Enrichment of the LTR region by TATA-binding protein (TBP) and acetylated lysine 27 histone H3 supports the involvement of this region in the transcription of POU5F1/OCT4.
source: Additionally, enrichment of this LTR region by TATA-binding protein (TBP) and acetylated lysine 27 histone H3 supports the involvement of this region in the transcription of POU5F1/OCT4.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' interpretation of published data.

claim: The LTR promoter region contains three consensus half-sites for HNF1A.
source: Interestingly, this LTR promoter region contains three consensus half-sites for HNF1A (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: HNF1A showed significant enrichment of two half-sites in NY5 and all three half-sites in NY8 and NY15 by ChIP-PCR.
source: To test whether HNF1A binds directly to these half-sites, ChIP-PCR was performed in NY5, NY8, and NY15 cells. Consistent with the ENCODE data we observed significant enrichment of two half-sites in NY5 and all three half-sites in NY8 and NY15 by HNF1A.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data.

claim: The canonical distal enhancer of POU5F1/OCT4 and HNF1A non-target gene MYOD showed no significant enrichment by HNF1A in ChIP-PCR.
source: By contrast, the canonical distal enhancer of POU5F1/OCT4 (Yeom et al., 1996), located 14-kbp downstream of the LTR promoter, and HNF1A non-target gene MYOD showed no significant enrichment by HNF1A (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating the specificity of enrichment observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Co-transfection of 293FT cells with the LTR reporter and an HNF1A-expression plasmid resulted in a 4.5-fold induction of Cypridina luciferase expression over LacZ-expression plasmid co-transfected cells.
source: To validate the LTR promoter region as an HNF1A-responsive promoter region, a reporter construct was generated encompassing the three putative HNF1A half-sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C). Co-transfection of 293FT cells (which lack endogenous HNF1A) with the LTR reporter and an HNF1A-expression plasmid resulted in a 4.5-fold induction of Cypridina luciferase expression over LacZ-expression plasmid co-transfected cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Neither the cloning vector nor the canonical downstream promoter region of POU5F1/OCT4 showed responsiveness to HNF1A expression.
source: Additionally, neither the cloning vector nor the canonical downstream promoter region of POU5F1/OCT4 showed responsiveness to HNF1A expression, supporting the POU5F1/OCT4 LTR promoter as the HNF1A-responsive promoter for the gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter assay data.

claim: Depletion of POU5F1/OCT4 resulted in a pronounced inhibition of tumorsphere formation, comparable to HNF1A knockdown.
source: To determine if POU5F1/OCT4 regulation was a key event in HNF1A-dependent stemness, we targeted POU5F1/OCT4 with multiple siRNAs, either in combination or as single sequences. Depletion of POU5F1/OCT4 resulted in a pronounced inhibition of tumorsphere formation, comparable to HNF1A knockdown (Figure 6D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumorsphere assay data shown in Figure 6D-H.

claim: POU5F1/OCT4 knockdown did not result in changes in apoptosis in NY8 cells.
source: To determine whether changes in apoptosis or cell cycle were responsible for the loss of tumorsphere formation in response to POU5F1/OCT4 knockdown, we performed annexin V/DAPI staining and propidium iodide staining in NY8 cells following transfection with POU5F1/OCT4 siRNA. Consistent with its role as a regulator of stemness in normal and cancer stem cells (Okita et al., 2007; Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006; Lu et al., 2013; Kumar et al., 2012; Nishi et al., 2014), we did not observe changes in either apoptosis or cell cycle in response to POU5F1/OCT4 knockdown (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by annexin V staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: POU5F1/OCT4 knockdown did not result in changes in cell cycle in NY8 cells.
source: we did not observe changes in either apoptosis or cell cycle in response to POU5F1/OCT4 knockdown (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by propidium iodide staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Knockdown of either HNF1A or POU5F1/OCT4 had comparable effects on the protein levels of OCT4A.

claim: Expression of OCT4A rescued the impaired tumorsphere formation caused by HNF1A depletion in NY8 and NY15 cells.

Consistent with our previous results, loss of HNF1A impaired tumorsphere formation in both lines expressing the vector control, however, this effect was rescued by the expression of OCT4A (Figure 6I, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by tumorsphere assay data shown in Figure 6I and Figure 6—figure supplement 2C,D.
